headline: Highest risk is capability conflict: AutoGen can write/execute locally while EMQX exposes broad network egress, creating default-path operational and data-handling hazards; prompt-injection and leakage are lower but present via shared…

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write files and run code, and its session scope is per-application process; EMQX exposes HTTP APIs and broad network egress. If AutoGen writes attacker-controlled content into a shared workspace that EMQX later consumes, instruction hijacking is plausible. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to share the same working directory or file drop location, injection becomes reachable.
IF EMQX consumes file-backed content produced by AutoGen without provenance checks, malicious instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent.
Disable file-based handoff between agents.
Add provenance tags to any shared artifacts.
Require human review before EMQX acts on AutoGen output.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing for shared inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen explicitly handles model provider API keys and reads/writes application files; EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace, sensitive application or IoT data can move from AutoGen into EMQX outputs or network traffic. The pairwise leak path is inferred, not directly documented, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem or message queue, data can cross from AutoGen to EMQX.
IF EMQX forwards received payloads over HTTP API or network egress, touched IoT data may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories.
Use separate service accounts and credentials.
Restrict EMQX egress to approved endpoints.
Redact API keys before any handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, install packages, and write the filesystem. EMQX has broad network egress and HTTP API access. If both operate on the same mutable resources, concurrent writes or side effects can collide; the profiles do not show locking or coordination, so the default risk is high rather than medium.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, package environment, or API-backed resource, conflicts can occur.
IF AutoGen installs packages while EMQX is running in the same environment, state drift may break either agent.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own container or VM.
Use read-only mounts where possible.
Avoid shared mutable directories.
Serialize access to any shared API resource.
requires-engineering: add distributed locking around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool outputs and code-derived facts; EMQX exposes HTTP APIs and network egress, so downstream automation could treat AutoGen output as authoritative. There is no documented verification step between them, making a cascading error plausible in default setups, but not clearly irreversible.
conditions: IF EMQX consumes AutoGen-generated text or JSON without validation, errors can propagate.
IF AutoGen produces incorrect facts that EMQX uses to trigger actions, downstream mistakes multiply.
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents.
Require schema checks on all AutoGen outputs.
Log and review any action-triggering payloads.
Limit EMQX to read-only consumption until verified.
requires-engineering: add confidence scoring and rejection rules.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and application data, while EMQX touches IoT data. The profiles do not show a residency, certification, or retention mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is visible. Because the pairwise compliance pathway is not documented, this stays low rather than medium.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is routed through a non-approved deployment of either agent, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF retention settings differ between the two systems for the same data class, deletion/export handling can diverge.
mitigations: Document data classes handled by each agent.
Align retention settings across both systems.
Avoid sending regulated data through unreviewed paths.
Review vendor and deployment residency before use.
requires-engineering: map each data class to a compliance control owner.
